questions.question: What is the primary goal of stroke imaging in the acute setting?
choices: To determine the exact age of the patient
To identify the specific molecular subtype of a tumor
To determine which patients would benefit from reperfusion therapy
To quantify the amount of old microangiopathy
To assess for spinal cord involvement
questions.detail: The primary objective of imaging in the acute stroke setting is to select candidates who will benefit from reperfusion treatments.

questions.question: Which imaging finding on MRI can help identify candidates for IV tPA when the 'last known normal' time is unclear?
questions.detail: A mismatch where lesions are positive on diffusion-weighted imaging but negative on FLAIR suggests the infarct is hyperacute, specifically less than 4.5 hours old, and may still benefit from thrombolysis.

questions.question: According to AHA guidelines, advanced imaging (CTP or MR perfusion) is recommended for selecting mechanical thrombectomy candidates in which time window?
questions.detail: For mechanical thrombectomy, advanced imaging like CT or MR perfusion is recommended to select candidates within the 6–24 hour window after they were last known to be normal.

questions.question: Large vessel occlusion (LVO) eligible for mechanical thrombectomy typically involves which segments?
choices: M1 segment of the MCA or intracranial ICA
questions.detail: Candidates for mechanical thrombectomy typically have occlusions in large vessels, specifically the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) or the intracranial internal carotid artery (ICA).

questions.question: Which clinical trial established the benefit of thrombectomy between 6–24 hours using 'clinical-core mismatch' as a criterion?
questions.detail: The DAWN trial demonstrated the benefits of performing thrombectomy 6 to 24 hours after the last known normal time by using clinical-core mismatch as a selection criterion.

questions.question: The 'infarct core' is defined as hypoperfused tissue that:
choices: Is at risk but salvageable with reperfusion
Is not salvageable regardless of subsequent reperfusion
Only occurs in the posterior circulation
Demonstrates T2 shine-through but normal ADC
questions.detail: The infarct core refers to tissue that has already sustained irreversible damage and cannot be salvaged even with successful reperfusion.

questions.question: Which perfusion parameter represents the tissue 'at risk' (ischemic penumbra)?
choices: Delayed contrast arrival (elevated Tmax) with compensated CBV
questions.detail: The ischemic penumbra, or tissue at risk, is characterized by delayed contrast arrival (elevated Tmax) while maintaining relatively compensated cerebral blood volume (CBV).

questions.question: In automated CT perfusion software, what is the established threshold for the infarct core?
questions.detail: Automated software typically defines the infarct core as tissue where the cerebral blood flow (CBF) is less than 30–45% compared to normal brain tissue.

questions.question: The central volume equation relates which three hemodynamic parameters?
questions.detail: The central volume equation states that cerebral blood flow (CBF) is equal to cerebral blood volume (CBV) divided by the mean transit time (MTT).

questions.question: A Tmax delay of greater than how many seconds is typically used to define the ischemic penumbra?
questions.detail: A delay in Tmax of more than 6 seconds is the standard threshold used to define hypoperfused tissue within the ischemic penumbra.

questions.question: The 'insular ribbon sign' on a noncontrast head CT refers to:
choices: Hyperdense thrombus in the M1 segment
Loss of gray-white differentiation in the insular cortex
questions.detail: The 'insular ribbon sign' is characterized by the loss of normal differentiation between gray and white matter in the insular cortex on a noncontrast CT scan.

questions.question: Which CT finding is specific for ischemia but only seen in approximately 1/3 of cases?
questions.detail: The 'hyperdense artery sign' is a specific indicator of acute ischemia, although it is only present in about one-third of stroke cases.

questions.question: What is the MRI correlate to the CT 'hyperdense artery sign'?
choices: Blooming artifact on GRE or SWI within a vessel
Bright T1 signal in the cortex
questions.detail: On MRI, the presence of blooming artifact within a vessel on GRE or SWI sequences corresponds to the hyperdense artery sign seen on CT.

questions.question: Within minutes of critical ischemia, why does DWI show reduced diffusivity?
choices: Failure of the Na/K ATPase pump leading to cytotoxic edema
questions.detail: Reduced diffusivity on DWI occurs very quickly after ischemia because the Na/K ATPase pump fails, leading to the development of cytotoxic edema.

questions.question: At what stage does an infarct typically show peak mass effect and sulcal effacement?
questions.detail: The mass effect and sulcal effacement associated with an infarct usually peak during the acute to early subacute stage, roughly 3 to 5 days after the event.

questions.question: In which phase of infarction does T2/FLAIR hyperintensity first reliably extend to involve the white matter?
choices: Never; it is restricted to gray matter
questions.detail: While early T2/FLAIR changes may be subtle, hyperintensity typically extends to include the white matter during the early subacute phase, between 1.5 and 5 days.

questions.question: 'Gyriform enhancement' in a late subacute infarct typically lasts for which duration?
questions.detail: Gyriform enhancement is a characteristic of late subacute infarcts and generally lasts from 6 days to about 6 weeks.

questions.question: According to the '2-2-2' rule for subacute infarct enhancement, when does the enhancement peak?
questions.detail: The '2-2-2' rule states that enhancement in a subacute infarct begins at 2 days, reaches its peak at 2 weeks, and typically fades by 2 months.

questions.question: How can a subacute infarct be distinguished from a tumor if both show enhancement?
choices: Infarcts lack significant mass effect at the time of enhancement
Infarcts always involve the corpus callosum
Only infarcts show Choline peaks on MRS
questions.detail: By the time a subacute infarct demonstrates enhancement, it typically lacks significant mass effect, which helps differentiate it from an enhancing tumor.

questions.question: Cortical laminar necrosis is characterized by lipid-laden macrophages and manifests as:
choices: Restricted diffusion with no T2 change
questions.detail: Cortical laminar necrosis involves the accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages and appears as hyperintensity on both T1 and T2-weighted MRI sequences.

questions.question: A 'V-shaped' midbrain infarct combined with bilateral ventromedial thalamic infarcts is pathognomonic for:
questions.detail: The combination of bilateral ventromedial thalamic infarcts and a 'V-shaped' midbrain infarct is a pathognomonic finding for an Artery of Percheron infarction.

questions.question: Which small vessel supplies the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule?
questions.detail: The recurrent artery of Heubner is responsible for supplying the head of the caudate and the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

questions.question: Occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery results in infarction of which structures?
choices: Optic chiasm, hippocampus, and posterior limb of the internal capsule
questions.detail: Anterior choroidal artery occlusions lead to infarcts involving the optic chiasm, the hippocampus, and the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

questions.question: Infarction of the bilateral thalami is a characteristic pattern for which two conditions?
choices: Deep venous system thrombosis or Artery of Percheron infarct
questions.detail: Bilateral thalamic infarction is typically caused by either deep venous system thrombosis or an infarction of the Artery of Percheron.

questions.question: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis characteristically causes infarction in the:
questions.detail: Thrombosis in the superior sagittal sinus classically results in venous infarction within the parasagittal high convexity cortex.

questions.question: The 'ivy sign' on FLAIR MRI is a marker of slow collateral flow in which condition?
questions.detail: The 'ivy sign' seen on FLAIR images is a marker of slow collateral flow characteristic of Moyamoya disease.

questions.question: CADASIL (an inherited small vessel arteriopathy) characteristically shows symmetric T2 hyperintensity in which specific location?
choices: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Anterior temporal lobes or paramedian frontal lobes
questions.detail: CADASIL typically presents with symmetric T2 hyperintensities located in the anterior temporal lobes or the paramedian frontal lobes.

questions.question: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is typically triggered by:
questions.detail: PRES is most commonly triggered by acute hypertension, eclampsia, or certain chemotherapy regimens.

questions.question: Which condition presents with 'stroke-like' migraine attacks years after radiotherapy?
questions.detail: SMART syndrome (stroke-like migraine attacks after radiation therapy) is a delayed complication of radiotherapy that can occur years later.

questions.question: Duret hemorrhages in the pons are a secondary complication of:
choices: Downward transtentorial herniation causing shearing of perforators
questions.detail: Duret hemorrhages in the pons occur when downward transtentorial herniation causes shearing of small perforating arteries.
